newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Turnout for Indonesian election re-vote well down.
newsitem.headline: Turnout for Indonesian election re-vote well down.

text.p: Indonesia's ruling Golkar party won an unprecedented re-vote on Madura island on Wednesday, just days after angry Moslems burned ballot boxes claiming fraud following last week's general elections.
Sampang Regency head Fadhilah Budiono said Golkar won 58 percent of ballots cast at the 65 polling stations where the new vote was held on the island off East Java.

The Moslem-backed United Development Party (PPP), whose supporters rioted after the May 29 poll on reports of a Golkar sweep, took 41.1 percent of the re-vote, while the other legal party, the fragmented Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), won 0.9 percent.
But the turnout dropped sharply on Wednesday to 59 percent compared to more than 90 percent in last week's poll.
Asked if he was disappointed, Budiono said: "The invitation to vote went out to all the village heads and through the mosques.
"I do not know why they did not come, because as good citizens we must use our right to vote."

Golkar, in power for much of President Suharto's 30-year rule and assured of victory before a ballot was cast, swept the national elections last week with more than 74 percent of the vote. The PPP got almost 23 percent and the PDI three percent.
The PPP and the PDI, as well as independent monitors, have charged that there were numerous irregularities during the campaign -- the most violent in three decades -- and the election itself.
Much of the violence involved rival partisans of the Golkar and the PPP, whose leaders were due to meet on Thursday to decide whether to accept the overall result.
Financial markets have been keeping a wary eye out for the PPP decision for fear that a rejection could lead to more violence, particularly in the capital, Jakarta.
Sampang, a sleepy coastal town of around 100,000, was quiet on Wednesday evening, with the result of the re-vote not yet generally known.
PPP supporters had burned or damaged houses, offices and other buildings and destroyed ballot boxes after the initial poll.
"If the rules are violated, then the people are unhappy. If they are obeyed, then they are happy," influential local Moslem leader Alawy Muhammad told Reuters.

Heavy security was in force for the re-vote, and the official Antara news agency reported East Java military commander Major-General Imam Utomo as having issued a shoot-on-the-spot order in case of further violence.
The PPP had said it would not provide witnesses for Wednesday's re-vote but stopped short of making an illegal call for a boycott.

But at the number six booth in Rongtengah, a devoutly religious area of Sampang with a number of Islamic schools, the head of the booth, Fattah, said there were 531 registered voters, of whom 506 voted last week.

On Wednesday, the only voters were the eight officials at the booth itself. "I don't know why they didn't come. The eight votes were only those of the polling station officials and witnesses," Fattah told Reuters.
